subject: maths

moments.title: Hilbert's 23 problems
moments.who: David Hilbert, International Congress of Mathematicians, Paris
moments.body:
At the 1900 ICM, David Hilbert presents a list of 23 outstanding mathematical problems that he believes will shape 20th-century mathematics. He doesn't present all 23 in his actual lecture (he speaks on 10); the full list appears in the printed version.

The problems span foundations, geometry, number theory, algebra, analysis, and physics. They become the most influential problem list in mathematical history.

quote.text: Wir müssen wissen — wir werden wissen. (We must know — we shall know.)

moments.takeaway: Hilbert sets the mathematical agenda for the 20th century with 23 carefully chosen problems.

moments.title: Solving Hilbert's problems
moments.body:
Over the next century, mathematicians chip away at the list. Some get solved relatively quickly (Hilbert's 3rd problem by Max Dehn in 1900). Some take decades or never get fully resolved.

Notable resolutions:
- 1st (Continuum Hypothesis): Gödel and Cohen show it's independent of ZFC (1940, 1963). Neither true nor false in standard axioms.
- 10th (Diophantine equations): Matiyasevich (1970) proves no general algorithm exists.
- 17th (sums of squares): Artin proves it (1927).
- 18th (sphere packing in 3D): Kepler conjecture, proved by Hales (1998-2014).
- 8th (Riemann hypothesis): still open. The most famous unsolved problem in mathematics.
moments.takeaway: Hilbert's problems drove an enormous amount of 20th-century mathematics. Most are resolved; a few remain open.

moments.title: Entscheidungsproblem
moments.body:
In 1928, Hilbert and Ackermann formally pose the Entscheidungsproblem (decision problem): is there a general algorithm to decide whether any mathematical statement is provable from a given set of axioms?

Hilbert believes the answer should be yes. This is the heart of his 'Hilbert program' — a complete, consistent, decidable formalisation of all mathematics.
moments.takeaway: Hilbert lays out the most ambitious foundational program in mathematics: make mathematics fully formalisable and mechanically decidable.

moments.title: Gödel and Turing demolish the program
moments.body:
Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931): any consistent formal system rich enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency.

Turing (1936) and Church (independently) prove the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable: there is no algorithm to decide truth in arithmetic. Turing's halting problem result implies it.

Hilbert's program is dead. The grand vision of decidable mathematics cannot be realised.
moments.takeaway: Two independent results overturn the heart of Hilbert's foundational program. Mathematics has provably unsolvable problems.

moments.title: Millennium Prize Problems
moments.body:
On the 100-year anniversary of Hilbert's list, the Clay Mathematics Institute announces seven 'Millennium Prize Problems', each worth $1 million for a solution:

- Riemann hypothesis (also Hilbert's 8th)
- P vs NP
- Yang-Mills existence and mass gap
- Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness
- Hodge conjecture
- Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
- Poincaré conjecture (solved by Perelman 2003)

Perelman solved the Poincaré conjecture and famously refused the $1M prize and the Fields Medal.
moments.takeaway: A century after Hilbert, a new list of grand challenges is set. Only one has been solved (and the solver refused the prize).

now.title: Hilbert's legacy today
now.body:
Hilbert's program failed, but it shaped 20th-century mathematics enormously. Formal logic, computability theory, proof theory, model theory, and reverse mathematics all descend from his foundational concerns.

Many of his 23 problems are solved; some are partially solved; a few (notably the Riemann hypothesis) remain open. The methodology of setting public problem lists to focus mathematical effort continues to be effective.
now.open_questions: Riemann hypothesis. P vs NP. The exact nature of computability. The deeper structure of arithmetic. Will any of the Millennium problems be solved in the 21st century at the rate Hilbert's were?

reflection: Hilbert was wrong about his deepest hope — mathematics is incomplete and undecidable. Yet his program drove most of 20th-century logic and computer science. Failed grand visions can be more productive than successful incremental ones. How should research communities decide which 'impossible' goals to chase?
